title: The heavens torn open (Mark 1:9–13)
hook: the sky rips, the Spirit comes down like a dove, then straight into the desert

segments.voice: Yesterday: gospel, good news, and a man in camel hair by the Jordan. Your line was the beginning of the good news. Did you read those first eight verses aloud? Day one hundred fifty-eight.

Yesterday John said someone mightier was coming. Today he arrives, and Mark gives him no introduction at all. No backstory. No childhood. Just: in those days Jesus came from Nazareth of Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan. One sentence. He walks down into the river with everyone else. Then he comes up out of the water, and something happens that Mark describes with a word so violent it's almost shocking. Not the sky opening politely, like curtains. The sky ripping. And then, before you've even caught your breath, it's over, and he's alone in the desert. Five verses. Today: the heavens torn open.
screen: `NO BACKSTORY, ONE SENTENCE.` → `INTO THE RIVER WITH EVERYONE.` → `THE SKY RIPS.`

segments.voice: The heavens torn open. The King James Bible says it gently: "And straightway coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens opened, and the Spirit like a dove descending upon him." But the Greek word Mark uses is schizō: to tear, to split, to rip. It's where we get the word schism. Matthew and Luke, telling the same scene, use the ordinary word for open. Mark says torn. And the verb comes back at the very end of Mark: when Jesus dies on the cross, the curtain of the Temple is torn in two from top to bottom. The same word. Beginning and end. Mark is framing his whole story: heaven ripped open to earth. Then a voice: "Thou art my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Notice when this comes. Before a single miracle. Before a sermon. Before he's done anything at all. Beloved first. And then, right away, the turn. "And immediately the spirit driveth him into the wilderness." Driveth. It's a strong word, the same one Mark later uses for casting out demons. The same Spirit that came down like a dove now drives him out. Forty days in the wilderness, tempted by Satan, with the wild beasts, and angels serving him. Mark gives none of the conversation with the tempter that Matthew and Luke tell. Just wild animals and angels, side by side. Some readers take comfort from the order: being beloved doesn't mean skipping the desert. Jesus heard the voice, and then went straight into the wilderness. In Mark, the voice comes first.
screen: `SCHIZŌ — THE SKY RIPS.` · `TORN AT THE START, TORN AT THE CROSS.` · `BELOVED, BEFORE HE'D DONE ANYTHING.` · `DRIVEN INTO THE WILDERNESS.` · then, large: `THOU ART MY BELOVED SON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Notice how fast Mark moves: river, sky, dove, voice, desert, all in a few breaths. Now slow it down. Picture the water. Picture coming up out of it. If you're a Christian, you might hear the voice as spoken to you too, through baptism: beloved. If you're not, you can simply notice what it would mean to be loved before you've done anything. Then think about the desert you're walking into this week. Let the first word go with you into it. The bell holds the time.
The heavens torn open. Mark's word is schizō, to rip, and he uses it again when the Temple curtain tears at the cross.
Your line: beloved, then the desert. Today, when something hard comes, remember that the voice came before the wilderness. Day one hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Many churches remember Jesus's baptism at the feast of the Baptism of the Lord or Theophany in January, and some lectionaries read Mark's desert verses at the start of Lent, when a season of forty days begins.

fork.reveal: "and immediately the spirit driveth him into the wilderness." beloved first, then the desert.

original.note: Greek: being torn apart — Mark's word for the heavens (1:10); schism comes from the same root.

trapdoor: what you thought: the sky opened and a dove came down.
what it means: the sky ripped, a voice said beloved, and the Spirit drove him straight into the desert.
what a scholar hears: schizomenous in 1:10 and eschisthē in 15:38 (the Temple veil) bracket Mark's gospel; Matthew and Luke soften it to opened.

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): 'only one other time' count softened (Mark 2:21 has the related noun schisma); stock line 'Christians have found comfort here for centuries' and the narrator's own theological claim reframed as what some readers take; howItsDone lectionary claim hedged.

Mark 1:10 σχιζομένους vs Matthew 3:16 and Luke 3:21 (ἀνοίγω, opened). Mark 15:38 ἐσχίσθη. 'Only one other time in his gospel': the verb schizō appears in Mark at 1:10 and 15:38; Mark 2:21 has the related noun schisma (a tear in cloth). Confirm the claim is limited to the verb.
Driveth: ἐκβάλλει, the verb Mark also uses for casting out demons. Confirm.
Practice links 'beloved' to baptism for Christians; kept as an invitation. Confirm.
howItsDone: the Baptism of the Lord (Western) / Theophany (Orthodox, January 6); Mark 1:9–15 is read on the First Sunday of Lent in Year B of the Revised Common and Catholic lectionaries. Confirm.
